The deputy must know the required work, have the necessary competence and access, understand the current authority limits and accept the period of responsibility. The executive and relevant colleagues should know when the deputy is acting and where to send requests.
Use the deputy's individual authorised access. Do not make continuity depend on copying passwords or forwarding every private message. A small, maintained support record can be more useful than a large archive of unfiltered correspondence. The record should point to the current programme, approvals, contacts and unresolved actions through the approved access structure.
Prepare for both planned and unplanned absence. During planned leave, a joint review may be possible. During an unexpected absence, the designated manager must be able to activate the approved cover arrangement without relying on the absent EA to reconstruct everything. A practice handover can reveal missing permissions and unclear ownership before the gap matters.
1.8.4 The handover that transfers responsibility
A handover is complete when the incoming owner can understand and accept the continuing work. A sent attachment is not enough. Confirm the scope, the time of transfer, any limitations and where unresolved matters go. Record acceptance in a proportionate way that the relevant people can retrieve.
Consider Meridian's afternoon site visit. In a later case update, the approved activity continues beyond Daniel's 17:00 finish. Aisha has agreed a defined administrative cover period and the control room has separately accepted monitoring under its fictional service arrangement. Daniel must give Aisha the current information and outstanding decisions, not simply say "the room is handling it."
The control room's role and the deputy's role may continue in parallel. The room may own monitoring and alert coordination while Aisha owns an administrative change or communication. The handover should not imply that one automatically replaces the other. Nor should a change to the EA cover period silently amend the provider's monitoring scope.
UK HSE's lone-working guidance includes agreed contact arrangements, monitoring and confirmation of return. Those principles are used here by analogy. The detailed executive-support handover model is a proposed course method, not a claim that every executive is a lone worker. [S6; R1, section 7]
BOUNDARY | When cover has not been accepted
Do not record a transfer that has not occurred. Escalate the gap to the appointed manager or duty owner, state what continues and request an explicit arrangement. The solution is neither silent abandonment nor an unspoken requirement that the outgoing EA remain responsible without limit.
1.8.5 Protect the assistant's own safety and judgement
The EA is part of the group the support arrangement should protect. Do not send an assistant to confront a threatening visitor, investigate an unexplained location or resolve an incident physically because they know the executive well. The companion awareness guide's people-first and non-investigative boundary remains applicable. [A1, p. 6]
A concern about workload, unsafe instructions or inadequate information should be raised before it becomes an error. State the observed problem and its consequence rather than diagnosing yourself or someone else. "I cannot complete both checks within the available time; one needs to be reassigned" is actionable. So is "the after-hours owner has not accepted the activity."
Managers should respond by clarifying priorities, authority and support rather than asking the assistant to hide uncertainty. The proposed course model treats a well-founded report of a gap as useful information. It does not promise that every organisation already has that culture; the working agreement should identify how concerns will actually be handled.
1.8.6 Review the relationship, not only the workload
A periodic review should ask whether the service still fits the executive's objectives, whether decisions arrive in time, whether the assistant can work within the agreed authority, and whether another authorised person can provide cover. Discuss changes in workload and the effectiveness of the communication rhythm.
Use a few meaningful examples. An unresolved approval that repeatedly arrives late may require a different decision route. A supplier repeatedly bypassing the agreed contact may need a clear joint message. An assistant who is asked for the same information in several places may need a better controlled record, not another reporting form.
Recognise useful independent judgement as well as speed. An assistant who identifies a gap and obtains the correct decision is not necessarily slower than one who marks every task complete. The latter may simply be transferring unrecognised risk and rework to other people.
Reflection 8. What must be true before you can say that a deputy has taken over an evening activity? Distinguish the deputy's acceptance from any continuing control-room responsibilities.

chapters.heading: 1.9 Putting the partnership into practice
chapters.label: 1.9 Putting the partnership into practice
chapters.sourceLocator: Editorial candidate 0.1 — 1.9 Putting the partnership into practice
chapters.text:
1.9.1 Revisit the Meridian morning
Daniel now applies the working method to the opening case. He does not start by assuming that every request must be accommodated. He reviews the approved programme, identifies the current priorities and prepares the decisions that Lindiwe actually needs to make.
The verified starting position is deliberately limited. Preparation is scheduled for 09:30 to 10:00. The decision meeting is 10:00 to 10:45. The client discussion is virtual at 11:30. The private commitment begins at 12:30. The afternoon site visit has accepted arrangements within its existing scope. The supplier request and lunch proposal are changes; they are not yet complete commitments.
Daniel records that the supplier's claimed approval is unverified and that the proposed lunch has not yet received the necessary consequential decisions. He does not infer that the existing site-visit arrangements cover it. He also does not seek the personal explanation behind the private time block merely to make the calendar easier to manipulate.
1.9.2 The conversation that resolves the business choice
Daniel gives Lindiwe a short brief. "The supplier's proposed time overlaps your preparation and the decision meeting. Their stated issue is a delivery sequence. I recommend asking operations to handle it and bring you any unresolved decision. The lunch option changes the venue and may conflict with your private block; it also needs revised protective and monitoring arrangements. Keeping the client discussion virtual preserves the current programme."
Lindiwe confirms that the decision meeting and private block remain. She authorises Daniel to ask the operations owner to handle the supplier discussion and chooses to retain the virtual client discussion. Daniel records those decisions. He then obtains the operations owner's acceptance and the client's confirmation of the original virtual arrangement. These later confirmations are explicit fictional case developments, not facts he was entitled to assume at the start.
Before the protected preparation period, the finance owner supplies the approved paper and Daniel checks its version against the pack record. This is a further fictional case development, not a confirmation he could assume earlier.
The afternoon visit remains unchanged. Daniel checks the current record rather than duplicating completed specialist work or announcing a new approval. The lesson is proportion: investigate the status of the relevant dependency, not every possible risk in the executive's life.
1.9.3 The professional record
A concise decision record is sufficient to show how the morning was resolved.
Matter | Decision or status | Owner and evidence
09:45 supplier request | Proposed executive appointment not accepted; discussion referred to operations after Lindiwe's approval. | Daniel records Lindiwe's decision and the operations owner's acceptance.
09:30 preparation | Retained. | Daniel records receipt and version-checking of the approved paper before preparation.
10:00 decision meeting | Retained. | Lindiwe remains the executive decision-maker; document owners retain their substantive responsibilities.
Client lunch proposal | Not taken forward; virtual discussion retained. | Daniel records the business decision and client's confirmation. No revised physical-venue approval is invented.
Private commitment | Protected time block retained. | No unnecessary personal detail is collected or distributed.
Afternoon site visit | Existing accepted scope retained; material changes would follow the agreed route. | Daniel refers to the current controlled arrangement.
The record separates decisions from their implementation. It also preserves the boundaries of Daniel's contribution. He has not made the investment decision, determined the supplier's delivery sequence or performed a protective assessment. He has made it easier for each appointed owner to do the right work.
1.9.4 A later handover
Later in the fictional day, a confirmed activity continues after Daniel's normal finish. Aisha has accepted administrative cover for the stated period and the control room's assigned duty holder has confirmed the monitoring record relevant to that activity. Daniel gives Aisha the current plan, references to the accepted service scope, open actions and the approved route for any unresolved decision.
Aisha confirms what she has accepted. Where a responsibility belongs to the control room, the handover states that explicitly rather than transferring it to her by implication. Daniel records the transition and informs the people who need to know whom to contact. The support arrangement continues because it was organised, not because Daniel remains privately available indefinitely.
1.9.5 What success looks like
There is no dramatic rescue in this case. No one is portrayed as incompetent or malicious. Success consists of a prepared executive, preserved commitments, an accepted delegation, limited disclosure and a support record that another person can use. Those ordinary outcomes are the foundation for more demanding work later in the programme.
The case also shows what remains outside the assistant's control. Another owner may deliver a paper late. A client may decline an alternative. A provider may have a genuine coverage limitation. The EA cannot guarantee those external actions. The professional response is to make the dependency visible, obtain a decision and avoid describing the unresolved matter as complete.
1.9.6 Five questions for your own practice
Before accepting a substantial support responsibility, ask these five questions.
Is the required result clear?
Do I have authority for the responsibility I am accepting?
Is the necessary information available?
Have competing demands been resolved?
Can the task be completed or properly handed over?
These questions express the unit's five supporting outcomes in everyday language. They are not a demand to produce a form for every conversation. With practice, they become a disciplined way of noticing what matters and bringing the right question to the right person.
KEY POINT | The partnership standard
A capable EA does not make uncertainty disappear by changing the wording. The EA makes uncertainty visible, assigns the appropriate decision and keeps the work moving within a clear mandate.

chapters.heading: Practical toolkit
chapters.label: Practical toolkit
chapters.text:
The following tools are original, reusable teaching templates. Complete them with fictional or sanitised information for learning. Before workplace use, reconcile them with the organisation's actual role descriptions, authority, privacy arrangements and service procedures. A completed form is evidence of a conversation or decision only when the relevant people have actually confirmed it.
Tool T1.1 - Executive support brief
Executive role and current business purpose: State the responsibilities and results the support arrangement must enable. Do not copy a job title without explaining the current work.
Priority and intended result: Identify the priority, why it matters now and the business result sought. Distinguish the result from an activity such as "hold a meeting."
EA deliverable and completion evidence: Define what you will produce or coordinate, who will use it and how its readiness will be checked.
Decision and input owners: Name roles for the substantive decision, required papers and other dependencies. Use a separate controlled directory for real personal contact details.
Review point and consequence of a gap: State when readiness will be reviewed, what happens if an input is late and who decides the alternative.
Capacity and support needs: Identify information, access, time, resources or deputy support that must be provided. Mark unconfirmed items as unconfirmed.
Tool T1.2 - Executive-EA working agreement
This blank structure follows the worked agreement in section 1.7. Complete each field with usable arrangements, not slogans. Extend a field when the role genuinely needs more detail; reference an existing controlled policy where it already answers the question.
Agreement area | Record the agreed arrangement
Identity and review | Agreement reference; executive and EA roles; version; effective point; review triggers; approving roles.
Purpose and priorities | Main support results; deliverables; decision points; method for resolving competing priorities.
Included and excluded work | Administrative scope; combined duties; specialist owners; explicitly excluded decisions or tasks.
Diary and information access | Required delegated access; protected blocks; minimum operational detail; restricted-information route.
Decision and spending authority | Independent actions; conditions and limits; approval owner; exceptions; distinction between ordering, approval and payment.
Communication | Routine review rhythm; approved channels; urgent route; capture of verbal decisions; fallback channel.
Confidentiality and personal tasks | Permitted work; verified recipients; information limits; family-liaison boundary; route for a new request.
Protective and monitoring interfaces | Required EPO decisions; actual service coverage; assignment acceptance; uncovered-activity escalation.
Availability and deputy | Duty periods; agreed additional coverage; deputy competence and access; explicit acceptance of each cover arrangement.
Concerns and handover | Routine decision route; alternative concern-reporting route; handover content; incoming acceptance; owner of a coverage gap.
Confirmation and changes | Confirming parties; outstanding dependencies; current-policy references; method for communicating a revised version.
Confirmation check: What part of the agreement depends on a person or service not yet consulted? Until that dependency is confirmed, do not describe the whole arrangement as operationally complete.
Tool T1.3 - Delegation and priority decision brief
The request: Describe the result sought, its source and the latest useful decision time. Identify any claimed approval that remains unverified.
Current commitments and constraints: State what would be displaced, which preparation or other dependency is affected and any policy, authority or service condition that applies.
Options: Set out feasible alternatives. For each one, explain what is preserved, what changes, the relevant cost or workload implication and what remains conditional.
Recommendation: Give a reason tied to the agreed business objective. Do not conceal an inconvenient consequence to make your preferred option look stronger.
Decision required: State who must decide and what the decision needs to cover. Separate the executive's business preference from a specialist decision or provider acceptance.
Implementation and closure: Record the actual decision, the people who must act, the acknowledgements needed and the evidence of completion or accepted transfer.
Tool T1.4 - Cover and handover record
Field | Information needed for a usable transfer
Assignment and period | Identify the work being transferred and the start and end of the cover period.
Current plan | Reference the current programme or record and explain material changes.
Authority and access | State what the incoming person may do and confirm usable individual access.
Open work | Record unresolved decisions, deadlines, dependencies and their owners.
Protective or service interfaces | Identify the accepted service scope and responsibilities that stay with the EPO, control room or other owner.
Exceptions and fallback | State the approved decision route and who owns a missing-coverage problem.
Acceptance and notification | Record the incoming person's acceptance and notify the people who need the new contact route.
Closure | Record completion or the next accepted transfer; do not close continuing work merely because the outgoing duty period ended.
Tool T1.5 - Partnership review conversation
Discuss one example of support that worked well and one example of avoidable friction. Ask whether the priorities were clear, whether the assistant had usable authority and information, whether changes were communicated and whether the work remained coverable. Identify a specific adjustment, its owner and the evidence that will show whether it helped.
Do not turn the review into a count of how often the assistant said yes or how rarely anyone reported a concern. The useful question is whether the arrangement enabled reliable work without concealing gaps or overloading a person. Retain only the information necessary for the review and follow the organisation's record-handling arrangements.
Working agreement response page
Use Tool T1.2 and the 12-clause worked example. Give a separate response to every area. These learning fields do not create an employment agreement, permission or service obligation.
Identity purpose and work scope
Record the learning agreement reference, version, roles, priorities and included or excluded work.
________________________________________________________________________________
Access decisions and spending
State permitted access and independent actions, conditions, limits and the separate approval or payment owner.
________________________________________________________________________________
Communication confidentiality and personal tasks
Define the channels, information limits, escalation and the route for a new personal task.
________________________________________________________________________________
Cover handover and specialist interfaces
Record the assignment and period, usable access, explicit acceptance and responsibilities retained by other owners.
________________________________________________________________________________
Confirmation and review
Identify each confirming role, unresolved dependency, effective point and review trigger. Mark absent evidence as unconfirmed.
________________________________________________________________________________

chapters.heading: Practice, reflection and explanatory guidance
chapters.label: Practice, reflection and explanatory guidance
chapters.sourceLocator: Editorial candidate 0.1 — Practice, reflection and explanatory guidance
chapters.text:
The unit practice task
Using the Meridian brief or another clearly fictional brief, produce a working agreement and a short priority-and-delegation exercise. Include the support objectives, authority boundaries, information access, communication preferences, personal-task limits, availability, escalation and deputy arrangements. Then explain your response to one competing-demand problem.
Your submission should make the distinction between proposed arrangements and confirmed facts explicit. A blank approval field is not a failure when the fictional brief has not supplied approval. Inventing an approval to make the form look finished is a failure of judgement. Identify who must confirm the outstanding matter and what cannot proceed as complete until they do.
Write your decision brief
Use the starting Meridian case before the later confirmations in section 1.9.2. Do not invent an approval. Refer to the worked agreement in section 1.7.3 and Tool T1.3.
Result and existing constraint
What is requested, and which commitment or preparation would it affect?
________________________________________________________________________________
Options and recommendation
State workable options, their consequences and the reason for your recommendation.
________________________________________________________________________________
Separate decisions and acceptance
Identify the business decision, any specialist input and each owner who must accept work.
________________________________________________________________________________
Unknowns and next review
What is not yet confirmed? Who must resolve it, by when, and what stays conditional?
________________________________________________________________________________
Use the following review guide. It is a learning aid, not the final course examination or a claim of workplace authorisation.
Supporting outcome | Evidence to look for
EA-01.1 | Priorities are translated into defined EA deliverables, named input or decision owners and useful review points.
EA-01.2 | The agreement addresses every specified area and identifies the authority or service dependencies that require confirmation.
EA-01.3 | The learner distinguishes neighbouring and specialist roles without assuming universal title-based powers.
EA-01.4 | Options are feasible, consequences are explained and conditional matters are not presented as already approved.
EA-01.5 | There is a usable concern-reporting route and an accepted cover process, not an assumption of permanent personal availability.
Guidance for Reflection 1 - Separate action from assumption
Daniel can review the current programme, identify conflicts, verify the supplier's request and prepare a decision brief. He can ask the relevant people for information through approved channels. He cannot yet claim that the supplier appointment, lunch transport or revised monitoring is confirmed. The executive must decide the business preference and any changed commitment; the relevant specialist and service owners must separately confirm matters within their responsibilities.
A strong answer does not treat the whole request as impossible. It identifies useful work that can proceed while preserving the status of the matters that remain unresolved.
Guidance for Reflection 2 - Access does not create approval authority
The assistant can identify the supplier process, confirm which owner may approve the exception and prepare the information that owner needs. Unless the actual delegation permits the approval, the assistant should not issue it simply because of proximity to the chief executive. A defensible response is helpful and specific: "I will route the request with its reason and deadline to the appointed approver; I am not authorised to approve that exception myself."
Guidance for Reflection 3 - Convert readiness into evidence
A useful support requirement identifies the decision being prepared, the agenda and approved papers needed, their owners, the preparation period and a readiness review. If an essential paper remains unapproved, the assistant flags it to the appropriate owner and executive, explains the effect on preparation and seeks the required decision. The assistant must not label a draft as approved or make the substantive decision personally.
Guidance for Reflection 4 - Correct the record and the action
An adequate message makes the corrected appointment time prominent, states that the earlier time is superseded and identifies any affected action such as transport or attendance. It reaches the people who must act and obtains the relevant acknowledgement. It does not include unnecessary personal information or hide the correction inside a long unrelated message. The controlled programme must also be corrected, not only the email.
Guidance for Reflection 5 - Define the routine boundary
A good delegation might permit changes to a routine internal catch-up within agreed available periods, provided no protected commitment, cost or specialist dependency is affected. It should refer a changed external venue, an affected executive decision meeting or a change involving additional expenditure to the appropriate owner. The record should include the result, scope, conditions, decision route, evidence and review point. The exact limits must come from the real or fictional brief, not from the learner's assumption.
Guidance for Reflection 6 - Keep approvals distinct
The lunch brief should show the proposed business benefit, the effect on the current programme and private block, and the alternative of retaining the virtual discussion. The physical option remains subject to the required protective input, transport arrangements and monitoring acceptance. No blanket waiting period or service guarantee should be invented. A recommendation is acceptable when its reason and conditions are explicit.
Guidance for Reflection 7 - Identify the other owners
Examples include finance confirming spending and payment controls, the information-access owner confirming delegated permissions, and the EPO or control-room owner confirming their actual role and service arrangements. HR or the designated manager may also need to confirm availability and cover arrangements. Lindiwe and Daniel can agree how they wish to work together, but they cannot create another function's authority or a provider's service obligation by writing it into their own document.
Guidance for Reflection 8 - Demonstrate accepted cover
The incoming deputy needs a defined assignment and period, usable access, current information, open actions and the relevant authority and escalation route. Acceptance must be explicit. The control room's monitoring role continues under its separately accepted mandate; it is not automatically transferred to the deputy. An unaccepted gap goes to the designated manager or duty owner for resolution rather than disappearing at the end of a shift.
Common weaknesses to correct
A weak agreement describes personal qualities but not decisions. A weak priority exercise says which request wins without explaining the consequence. A weak handover names a deputy but provides neither acceptance nor access. A weak role comparison assumes that a title grants authority. Correct these weaknesses by returning to the work itself: result, owner, conditions, evidence and the next decision.
A serious boundary error should be corrected and the relevant task demonstrated again. The aim is not to punish a learner for recognising uncertainty. It is to prevent unsafe or unsupported decisions from being hidden by a polished form or by strong performance on an unrelated question. [R2, assessment-design recommendations]

chapters.heading: Unit summary and key terms
chapters.label: Unit summary and key terms
chapters.sourceLocator: Editorial candidate 0.1 — Unit summary and key terms
chapters.text:
The foundation you have built
Executive support begins with the purpose of the work. The assistant translates that purpose into deliverables, protects preparation and makes dependencies visible. Reliability depends on explicit priorities, authority, information access, communication and cover.
The working agreement records a shared understanding, not merely a signature. It must help people respond to conflicting requests and absence. The EA coordinates with the EPO and control room without taking over their responsibilities. Carry that distinction into every later unit; LU2 develops the boundaries in detail.
Key terms used in this unit
Term | Meaning in this book
Authority | Permission to make a specified decision or perform an action within defined conditions.
Commitment | Work or an arrangement that has been accepted by the appropriate party, not merely requested.
Controlled record | The identified current record maintained through an agreed process, with material changes traceable.
Delegation | Assignment of defined work or decision rights with scope, limits and a completion expectation.
Dependency | An input, decision, resource or action on which another task depends.
Executive Protection Officer (EPO) | The appointed protection professional whose decisions and activities remain within the actual mandate.
Handover | An explicit transfer of defined continuing work to an incoming owner who accepts it.
Independent remote control room | The monitoring and coordination facility described in the programme; its powers and coverage depend on its real service mandate.
Mandate | The agreed scope and authority of a role, read with the applicable organisational requirements.
Priority | Work whose relative importance and timing have been considered against the agreed objectives and constraints.
Protective coordination | The EA's authorised organisation of information, decisions and interfaces that support the protective arrangement.
Working agreement | A practical record of how the executive-support partnership operates within existing authority and policy.

narrationText.D01-intro: Welcome and your practical destination. A professional executive partnership makes work clear and commitments reliable. In this unit you will translate priorities into support deliverables, prepare a usable working agreement, distinguish role boundaries, present options when demands conflict, and arrange a concern route and sustainable cover. Your two main work products are a working agreement and a priority decision brief. The Meridian people and arrangements are fictional. Numerical examples are case facts, not operating standards. The course does not grant workplace authority.. Start with the introduction video, then continue to the first reflection.
narrationText.D01-takeaway: Key takeaway. Your destination is a usable working agreement and a reasoned priority brief. Course examples are fictional and do not give you workplace authority.
narrationText.D02-intro: A Monday request before anything is confirmed. Daniel receives a message at 07:40. Lindiwe asks him to fit in a supplier and move the virtual client discussion to lunch at the client’s venue. The supplier claims approval for 09:45, but this is unverified. Existing accepted arrangements cover the afternoon site visit within its current scope. They do not establish cover for the proposed lunch. Before seeing later case developments, separate what Daniel can do now from what needs another person’s decision.. Write what Daniel can do now, two unknowns and who must decide. Attempt a response before opening the learning guidance.
narrationText.D02-takeaway: Key takeaway. Useful checking and preparation can proceed while approvals remain unknown. Do not turn a supplier’s claim, a lunch proposal or an assumed transport arrangement into a confirmation.
narrationText.D02-prompt: At 07:40, what can Daniel do now? Record two unknowns and identify who must decide.
narrationText.D02-guidance: Daniel can check the programme, verify the supplier request and prepare options. The supplier appointment, physical lunch, transport and revised monitoring are not confirmed. Lindiwe decides the business preference within her authority; Thandi owns protective input and the control room accepts its own monitoring scope.
narrationText.D03-intro: Turn the executive brief into reliable support. Reliable support begins with the business result, not a full calendar. Sending an invitation is an activity. A controlled ready pack is an output. A decision based on reliable information is the intended outcome. Use six briefing questions to define the result, its timing, the executive’s contribution, readiness, input owners and completion evidence. A missing paper, missing approval or capacity conflict stays visible.. Explore a worked support brief; then complete a short T1.1 example for the decision pack.
narrationText.D03-takeaway: Key takeaway. Readiness needs an agreed deliverable, named owners, a review point and reliable evidence. Invitations and draft papers alone do not prove that the decision pack is ready.
narrationText.D03-p1: Define the result. Ask what should be different after the work. Sending invitations is an activity; a confirmed meeting pack is an output; a decision based on reliable information is the intended business outcome. Daniel supports the decision without taking it over.
narrationText.D03-p2: Ask why now. Identify the useful decision time, consequences of delay and dependencies. Seniority does not make two simultaneous appointments feasible. Immediate danger uses the appropriate emergency route.
narrationText.D03-p3: Identify the executive contribution. Ask which decision or contribution requires the executive. Do not fill the diary before understanding the purpose. For the service investment, Lindiwe decides; finance and operations own their submissions.
narrationText.D03-p4: Define readiness. Specify the approved agenda, referenced papers, participants and preparation needed. A draft financial appendix must not be labelled approved. A complete cover sheet does not close a missing-paper gap.
narrationText.D03-p5: Name input owners. Agree who supplies each input, when and through which controlled record. Where several executives share an assistant, show realistic capacity and ask the designated manager to resolve competing demands without disclosing confidential content.
narrationText.D03-p6: Set review and evidence. Agree a pack-readiness review before preparation. If a paper is late or unapproved, make the gap and consequence visible and obtain the necessary decision. Use T1.1 to record result, deliverable, owners, review and capacity.
narrationText.D04-intro: A role title is not a grant of authority. Role titles vary and can overlap. An EA, PA, office manager, chief of staff and specialist adviser may work closely, but proximity to an executive does not transfer another role’s mandate. Production, judgement and coordination are connected contributions, not ranks. Compare what each role has actually been appointed to do before deciding where a request belongs.. Compare responsibilities and identify the appointed owner for a task that goes beyond Daniel’s role.
narrationText.D04-takeaway: Key takeaway. EA and PA roles can overlap. Executive access does not give you a chief-of-staff or specialist mandate. Refer a decision to its appointed owner while helping the legitimate task move forward.
narrationText.D04-p1: Executive Assistant. Coordinates defined executive-support work and makes the administrative judgements actually delegated. Production, judgement and coordination reinforce each other: prepare the pack, spot an unapproved appendix and obtain the correct paper from its owner. These contributions are not ranks.
narrationText.D04-p2: Personal Assistant. May provide overlapping professional or personal support. The title alone does not establish seniority, domestic duties or authority. Agree the actual work, resources and limits.
narrationText.D04-p3: Office manager. May own workplace resources, office services and wider administrative arrangements. Liaise with that owner unless the roles have expressly been combined. Combined duties still need specific permissions.
narrationText.D04-p4: Chief of staff. May hold a wider organisational or strategic mandate. Access to the executive does not confer this mandate on an EA. Conveying approved wording is different from negotiating a commitment.
narrationText.D04-p5: Specialist adviser. Provides appointed professional advice or decisions. The EA can prepare information, coordinate access and follow up without replacing finance, legal, procurement, protection or another specialist. Apply legitimate processes fairly.
narrationText.D04-prompt: A manager asks you to approve a supplier exception because you have direct executive access. What useful assistance can you provide without assuming approval authority?
narrationText.D04-guidance: Find the appointed approver, prepare the reason and deadline, and route the request. Direct access does not grant approval authority. The role comparison is a conversation aid, not a universal hierarchy.
narrationText.D05-intro: Communicate clearly and recover from an error. Trust should make a useful question easier to ask. Agree a communication rhythm, approved channels and a fallback. Distinguish receipt, decision and completion. When you make an error, correct the message and the controlled record and confirm that the affected people can act on the correction. A concern involving the executive needs an appropriate alternative reporting route.. Choose a helpful clarification, then draft a concise correction to an appointment time. Identify an alternative concern route if the executive is the subject of the concern.
narrationText.D05-takeaway: Key takeaway. Receipt, decision and completion are different states. Correct the message and the controlled record, and confirm that affected people can act on the correction. Keep private explanations private.
narrationText.D05-p1: Receive and clarify. Agree a communication rhythm, approved channels and an alternative if the normal channel fails. Record practical work preferences, not personality labels or gossip. Acknowledge receipt without describing it as approval or completion.
narrationText.D05-p2: Present a useful choice. Use constructive candour: state the shared objective, the facts, the conflict, workable options and the decision needed. Do not shorten “possible, subject to approval” into “arranged”.
narrationText.D05-p3: Capture the decision. Record material verbal decisions in the controlled record. Share sensitive information only with appropriate recipients. A private block may show unavailability without revealing its personal purpose.
narrationText.D05-p4: Correct an error openly. Establish the facts and consequences, inform the appropriate people, make the corrected time prominent and mark the earlier time superseded. Correct the controlled programme as well as the message; obtain acknowledgement from people who must act.
narrationText.D05-p5: Review and raise concerns. Review whether the cause was unclear information, inaccessible approval, checking failure or capacity. Use an alternative organisational route if the concern involves the executive. Immediate help must not wait for routine administrative approval.
narrationText.D06-intro: Check four conditions before accepting work. Keep four conditions separate: competence, authority, information and access, and capacity. Knowing how to do a task or having system access does not mean you may approve it. Record the result, scope, conditions, decision route, completion evidence and review or expiry of a delegation. Use individual authorised access rather than shared passwords.. Open each labelled condition and identify what remains missing in a supplier-record example.
narrationText.D06-takeaway: Key takeaway. Competence, authority, information and capacity are separate conditions. System access is not permission to approve a supplier bank-detail change.
narrationText.D06-p1: Competence. Can I perform this work to the required standard? Knowing how to edit supplier records is not authority to approve a bank-detail change. Refer the verification and decision to the appointed finance owner.
narrationText.D06-p2: Authority. Am I permitted to make this decision or act under the specific delegation? Permission to arrange is not automatically permission to approve, pay, disclose or direct a specialist.
narrationText.D06-p3: Information and access. Do I have the necessary facts and approved individual access? Use delegated access, not the executive’s password. A deputy receives the information needed for the accepted cover period, not an unrestricted archive.
narrationText.D06-p4: Capacity. Are enough time and resources available? Name a gap rather than promising simultaneous completion or hiding extra work. A senior instruction does not supply missing resources.
narrationText.D06-p5: The delegation record. Record six fields: result; scope; conditions; decision route; evidence; review or expiry. Routine internal meeting changes may be delegated only within the stated conditions. A changed external venue or executive decision meeting needs the appropriate decision.
narrationText.D07-intro: Act seek approval refer or decline. Choose a response to the exact action and its conditions. Act when the task is authorised and all conditions are met. Seek approval for a legitimate exception to your limit. Refer a specialist decision to its appointed owner. Decline and escalate an action that conflicts with a control you cannot override. The fictional R2,000 consumables example is conditional ordering authority, not payment authority.. Classify four short requests, then explain the decisive condition. Use labelled selection controls rather than a drag-only task.
narrationText.D07-takeaway: Key takeaway. Choose act, seek approval, refer, or decline and escalate according to the exact action and its conditions. The fictional R2,000 ordering limit is conditional; it is not payment authority and cannot be bypassed by splitting purchases.
narrationText.D07-routine: . Move a routine internal catch-up within an agreed free period. No protected commitment, external undertaking, cost or specialist dependency is affected; the actual delegation permits it.
narrationText.D07-spending: . An order exceeds the fictional R2,000 pre-approved meeting-consumables limit. The need is legitimate, but additional spending has not been approved.
narrationText.D07-bank: . A supplier requests a change to banking details. Daniel can edit the system but has no authority to approve the change.
narrationText.D07-private: . Someone asks Daniel to share the full private diary and family information without permission, contrary to the information control.
narrationText.D07-correctFeedback: Act only when all conditions are met. Seek the proper approval for a limit exception; refer specialist decisions; decline and escalate an unauthorised disclosure. The fictional R2,000 ordering example is conditional, is not payment authority and cannot be bypassed by splitting purchases.
narrationText.D07-incorrectFeedback: Assess the exact action and its conditions, not the requester’s seniority. Referral does not mean abandonment: record the owner and deadline while keeping the unresolved status visible.
narrationText.D08-intro: Read the diary without hiding the conflict. Read the diary precisely. Preparation is 09:30 to 10:00; the decision meeting is 10:00 to 10:45. The supplier requests 09:45 to 10:15. This overlaps fifteen minutes of each existing commitment. Do not hide either conflict, shorten preparation silently or present the unverified request as an accepted booking.. Inspect each overlap and say which work would be displaced. Distinguish an appointment request from an accepted booking.
narrationText.D08-takeaway: Key takeaway. The supplier request overlaps 15 minutes of preparation and 15 minutes of the decision meeting. Both conflicts stay visible. The claimed approval is still unverified.
narrationText.D08-p1: Preparation 09:30 to 10:00. This is verified preparation time. The supplier requests 09:45 to 10:15, so its first 15 minutes displace the final 15 minutes of preparation. Do not conceal this loss by shortening the block.
narrationText.D08-p2: Decision meeting 10:00 to 10:45. The final 15 minutes of the supplier request overlap the first 15 minutes of the decision meeting. Changing that meeting is outside Daniel’s routine delegation.
narrationText.D08-p3: A request is not a booking. The supplier says Lindiwe expects to see them. That claim is unverified. Confirm the purpose and decision needed before presenting options; do not mark the appointment accepted.
narrationText.D09-intro: Recommend a workable option without promising it. There may be more than one defensible recommendation. Operations might handle the delivery-sequence discussion if the required delegation and acceptance are obtained. A later executive slot may work if it meets the useful decision time. Changing the morning needs an explicit decision about its consequences. Lunch at another venue is a separate business, protective and service-scope question. Explore the conditions without inventing a reply.. Choose an option, state its conditions and distinguish the executive’s business choice from EPO input and room acceptance. Explore a different route after feedback.
narrationText.D09-takeaway: Key takeaway. A defensible option identifies what it preserves, its consequences and the conditions still outstanding. One person’s business approval does not supply another owner’s specialist decision or service acceptance.
narrationText.D09-node-supplier: The supplier needs a decision on delivery sequence, not a new commercial commitment. Which option will you take forward?
narrationText.D09-choice-operations: Recommend that operations handle the discussion, subject to the required delegation and acceptance.
narrationText.D09-feedback-operations: This can preserve preparation and the decision meeting. Lindiwe’s approval where required and the operations owner’s acceptance remain conditions, not supplied facts.
narrationText.D09-choice-later: Explore a later executive slot and check the latest useful decision time.
narrationText.D09-feedback-later: This can preserve morning commitments if the supplier accepts a feasible alternative. Do not promise a slot before checking availability and the decision deadline.
narrationText.D09-choice-change: Ask Lindiwe to decide whether to change the existing morning commitments.
narrationText.D09-feedback-change: Make the loss of preparation and effect on participants explicit. Daniel does not make this change under routine diary authority.
narrationText.D09-choice-assume: Confirm 09:45 because the supplier says it was approved.
narrationText.D09-feedback-assume: Stop: the claimed approval is unverified and two commitments conflict. Restore the pending status and prepare a decision brief.
narrationText.D09-node-repair: Which repair preserves an honest record?
narrationText.D09-choice-correct: Clarify that the slot is pending; verify the claim and present the conflicts.
narrationText.D09-feedback-correct: Correct the recipients’ understanding and the current record. Do not quietly replace an attachment.
narrationText.D09-node-lunch: What can be said about moving the virtual client discussion to lunch at another venue?

narrationText.D09-feedback-conditional: These are separate decisions. Existing afternoon arrangements do not automatically cover the proposed lunch.
narrationText.D09-choice-virtual: Recommend retaining the virtual discussion, explaining why and asking for the business decision.

narrationText.D10-intro: Write the priority and delegation brief. Write a short priority decision brief using the starting facts. Explain the requested result and existing constraint, compare feasible options, give a recommendation and reason, identify the decision required, and state what remains conditional. Keep business approval, protective input and monitoring acceptance separate. Retain this first draft before opening the later fictional update.. narrationText.D10-takeaway: Key takeaway. A useful brief makes the result, constraints, options, recommendation, required decision and unresolved conditions clear. Keep the first brief separate from the later case confirmations.
narrationText.D10-prompt: Draft six parts: requested result; current constraints; feasible options; recommendation and reason; the decisions required; unresolved conditions. Use only the starting facts. Save or acknowledge your first draft before the later case update.
narrationText.D10-guidance: Identify both 15-minute overlaps. Separate Lindiwe’s business choice from Thandi’s protective input and control-room acceptance. A recommendation is not a decision, and a decision is not completed implementation. Do not invent a reply, transport approval or accepted coverage. Use T1.3 to retain the actual decision and closure evidence when available.
narrationText.D11-intro: Build an agreement people can use. A working agreement helps people act within actual authority, policy and service arrangements. It does not replace those controls. The Meridian example has an identity and effective point plus twelve worked clauses. Explore each group and check which finance, access and service owners must confirm their parts. The eleven fields in Tool T1.2 combine some clauses; use the crosswalk so nothing is lost.. Review five groups: purpose/scope; access/decision/spending; communication/privacy/personal tasks; availability/cover/concerns; confirmation/change/review. Identify who else must confirm each relevant commitment.
narrationText.D11-takeaway: Key takeaway. A working agreement must help people act, not simply look signed. Check every worked clause against the tool fields, and identify the other owners whose confirmations are still needed.
narrationText.D11-identity: Identity and effective point. Agreement identity and purpose. Record MP-01, version 1.0, applies to executive support for Lindiwe by Daniel. Its purpose is to support timely business decisions, accurate communication and coordinated commitments. It becomes effective in the fictional case only after the required parties confirm their responsibilities. It is reviewed after the first working month and whenever scope, personnel, systems or material service arrangements change.
narrationText.D11-p1:
Purpose and scope. 1. Priorities and deliverables. Lindiwe confirms the current priority list and identifies decisions that require her attention. Daniel translates the list into a programme, preparation requirements, an action register and review points. For the Monday example, the decision pack and 09:30 preparation period are protected. Daniel identifies missing inputs; he does not approve the substantive financial or operational papers himself.

2. Scope of work. Daniel coordinates the diary, routine correspondence, meeting preparation, travel administration, relevant supplier follow-up and the administrative interfaces with the EPO and control room. Office facilities remain with the office-services owner. Contract interpretation remains with the designated legal or procurement owner. Public statements remain with the authorised communications function. Substantive business decisions stay with their appointed owners.
narrationText.D11-p2:
Access decisions and spending. 3. Diary access and protected information. Daniel receives approved delegated access sufficient to coordinate availability and business arrangements. Private commitments may appear as unavailable periods without a personal explanation. Where a private commitment affects agreed protective coverage, the necessary operational information goes through the approved restricted route. The existence of a protected block is not permission to investigate its purpose or disclose its detail.

4. Routine decision authority. Daniel may arrange and move routine internal administrative meetings within agreed available periods when no protected commitment, external undertaking, cost or specialist dependency is affected. Changes to executive decision meetings, external visits or protected periods require the identified decision-maker's approval. A request received directly by Lindiwe is entered into the controlled process before others are told that consequential arrangements are complete.

5. Spending and supplier authority. In this fictional example only, Daniel may place orders for pre-approved meeting consumables up to R2,000 per event within an already approved budget and supplier process. He may not split purchases to avoid the limit. He may prepare a quotation comparison for larger expenditure but may not approve it or release payment. A change to supplier payment details goes to finance through the approved independent verification route. The executive's preference for a supplier does not remove these conditions.
narrationText.D11-p3:
Communication privacy and service interfaces. 6. Communication and decisions. A short alignment conversation takes place at a time agreed for the working day. Routine tasks are recorded in the approved task system. Material instructions given verbally are captured in the appropriate record. Daniel distinguishes receipt, approval and completion in status messages. A sensitive matter uses a restricted channel. Silence or a message read receipt is not treated as approval of a new commitment.

7. Changes and protective interfaces. Daniel identifies which changes affect the programme, transport, venue or support arrangements. Lindiwe decides the business preference within her authority. Thandi, the EPO, owns the required protective input. The remote control room accepts the relevant monitoring assignment under its actual mandate. Daniel maintains the administrative status and escalates unaccepted or uncovered activity. None of these parties is recorded as having approved another party's decision.

8. Confidentiality and family or personal tasks. Daniel uses only the information needed for the authorised task and limits distribution to appropriate recipients. In the fictional scope, he may coordinate agreed personal appointments or family administrative contact where the necessary permission and time have been established. He is not the household investigator, family dispute mediator or automatic incident spokesperson. New personal tasks are considered against scope, privacy, resources and competing business work before being accepted.
narrationText.D11-p4:
Availability cover and concerns. 9. Availability and cover. Daniel's fictional normal support period is 08:00 to 17:00. This is a case fact, not an employment recommendation. Any planned work outside that period requires an agreed arrangement. Aisha is the appointed deputy for accepted cover periods, using her own authorised access. The control room's monitoring coverage is separately defined and does not depend on Daniel personally watching a phone after work. Neither the existence of Aisha nor the word "deputy" means that she has accepted every future assignment.

10. Concerns and unresolved decisions. Routine priority conflicts go to Lindiwe or the designated substitute decision-maker. Concerns involving personal safety, improper conduct or the executive herself have an alternative organisational reporting route identified in the controlled contact register. Daniel reports missing authority, information or service acceptance with the consequence and the decision required. Essential emergency help is not delayed to complete a routine administrative approval chain.

11. Handover and continuing activity. A handover identifies the current plan, open decisions, commitments, information location, relevant service acceptance and the named incoming owner. That person confirms acceptance. The outgoing and incoming roles are recorded separately from the control room's ongoing responsibilities. If cover is not accepted, Daniel escalates to the duty manager or designated owner; the unresolved obligation is not silently closed or indefinitely assigned to him by default.
narrationText.D11-p5: Confirmation change and review. 12. Review and confirmation. The parties review whether the agreement matches work as performed. They examine unresolved decisions, avoidable rework, late uncommunicated changes, unowned tasks and the usability of cover. They do not use low incident-report numbers as proof that the arrangement is sound. Amendments are versioned, approved by the appropriate owner and communicated to affected people. The executive and EA confirm the agreement; finance, information-access and support-service owners confirm the parts that depend on their authority. No fictional signature is represented as a real approval.
narrationText.D12-intro: Repair an agreement that sounds finished. An agreement can look finished while hiding a serious gap. Look for unlimited duties, assumed monitoring, payment rights that were not delegated, and automatic after-hours availability. Replace each vague promise with defined work, conditions, an owner and the required confirmation. A clause that honestly records a limit or an unknown is not defective for that reason.. Select every clause needing correction; explain one repair in your own words.
narrationText.D12-takeaway: Key takeaway. Repair unlimited duties, assumed service coverage, invented payment authority and automatic after-hours availability. A precise limit or an honest unknown is better than an unsupported promise.
narrationText.D12-prompt: Which clauses need correction? Select every clause that makes an unsupported or unlimited commitment.
narrationText.D12-correctFeedback: The first four clauses need repair. Define scope, obtain actual service-owner confirmation, distinguish ordering from payment, and agree cover periods and explicit acceptance. The final clause has a usable boundary. Test an agreement with an ordinary change and version material amendments.
narrationText.D12-incorrectFeedback: Look for an unlimited duty, a service promise made for someone else, a payment power not delegated and automatic after-hours cover. A precise conditional clause is not a defect simply because it limits authority.
narrationText.D12-all: Daniel handles everything the executive needs, without any limit.
narrationText.D12-room: The control room provides continuous cover because Lindiwe and Daniel wrote this into their agreement.
narrationText.D12-pay: Daniel’s conditional R2,000 ordering limit also authorises him to release payment.
narrationText.D12-hours: Aisha is deputy, so she and Daniel are automatically available after hours.
narrationText.D12-bounded: Routine internal changes may be made only within delegated conditions; exceptions go to the identified decision-maker.
narrationText.D13-intro: Make cover an accepted arrangement. Cover is an accepted arrangement, not permanent personal availability. Define the assignment and period, check the deputy’s competence and individual access, and transfer the current plan and open work. Keep administrative cover separate from the EPO’s input and the room’s monitoring. Record explicit acceptance and notify the people who need the new contact route. Escalate an unaccepted gap to the designated owner.. Walk through the handover sequence and identify the owner of an unaccepted gap.
narrationText.D13-takeaway: Key takeaway. A transfer needs a defined assignment, usable access and explicit acceptance. A sent attachment is not enough. Escalate an unaccepted gap without abandoning work or assuming unlimited personal availability.
narrationText.D13-p1: Define the assignment and period. Continuity is not permanent personal availability. Name the work and the start and end of administrative cover. Personal tasks must be agreed against scope, privacy, resources and competing business work.
narrationText.D13-p2: Check authority and access. The deputy needs competence, the specific authority and usable individual access. Do not share passwords or forward an unrestricted private archive. Plan for unexpected as well as planned absence.
narrationText.D13-p3: Transfer the current work. Reference the current programme, approved decisions, open actions, owners, deadlines and unresolved gaps. The incoming person needs a usable record, not only a large sent attachment.
narrationText.D13-p4: Keep service interfaces separate. Thandi’s protective input and the control room’s accepted monitoring remain under their own mandates. Administrative cover neither replaces them nor silently extends their scope.
narrationText.D13-p5: Obtain acceptance and notify. The incoming owner confirms the assignment and limitations. Notify people who need the new contact route. Receipt is not acceptance. Do not record a transfer that has not happened.
narrationText.D13-p6: Resolve gaps and review. Escalate unaccepted cover to the designated manager or duty owner. Do not silently abandon continuing work or assume unlimited outgoing availability. Use emergency routes for immediate danger. Review capacity, changes and coverability through T1.5.
narrationText.D14-intro: A deputy’s name is not enough. Aisha is appointed as deputy. Before the later update, that fact does not establish acceptance of this evening assignment. Identify the evidence that would make transfer usable, and distinguish administrative cover from responsibilities retained by the control room. Naming a person or sending an attachment does not complete a handover.. Write the evidence needed for transfer and what stays with the independent control room.
narrationText.D14-takeaway: Key takeaway. Naming a deputy does not confirm acceptance of a particular assignment. Keep the deputy’s administrative role separate from the room’s accepted monitoring responsibilities.
narrationText.D14-prompt: Before any later fictional update: Aisha is the appointed deputy, but acceptance of this assignment has not been supplied. What evidence is needed for transfer, and which responsibilities stay with the control room?
narrationText.D14-guidance: Define the assignment and period, competence, usable individual access, current plan, open actions, limits and the explicit incoming acceptance. The control room retains separately accepted monitoring and coordination under its mandate. If cover remains unaccepted, escalate the gap to the appointed owner; a deputy’s name alone is not a completed transfer.
narrationText.D15-intro: Now compare the later confirmed record. This is the later fictional case update, released after your first brief. Lindiwe keeps preparation, the decision meeting, the virtual client discussion and her private block. She authorises asking operations, and operations then accepts. The approved paper arrives and Daniel checks its version. Later, defined administrative cover and separately accepted monitoring are recorded. Compare these new facts with what was unknown at the start.. Compare your own brief with each decision and its implementation evidence. Explain what changed from unknown to confirmed, and who confirmed it.
narrationText.D15-takeaway: Key takeaway. The later record adds explicit business decisions, operations acceptance, client confirmation, paper verification and accepted cover. These developments must not be projected backwards into the starting facts.
narrationText.D15-p1: Later fictional update: the business choice. Only now does Lindiwe confirm that preparation, the decision meeting and the private block remain. She authorises asking operations to handle the supplier discussion and retains the virtual client discussion. These are later case facts, not assumptions available at 07:40.
narrationText.D15-p2: Operations and client acceptance. Daniel then obtains the operations owner’s acceptance and the client’s confirmation of the original virtual arrangement. Authorisation to ask is different from the recipient’s acceptance. No revised lunch venue approval is invented.
narrationText.D15-p3: Approved pack verified. Before preparation, finance supplies the approved paper. Daniel checks the version against the pack record. Receipt and version checking are explicit later fictional developments. Daniel does not approve the paper’s substance.
narrationText.D15-p4: The site-visit scope remains. The afternoon visit is unchanged within its accepted scope. Daniel checks the current record rather than duplicating specialist work or announcing a new approval.
narrationText.D15-p5: A later accepted handover. Later, Aisha accepts a defined administrative cover period and the assigned room duty holder confirms the relevant monitoring record. Daniel hands over the plan, service references and open work, records acceptance and notifies the appropriate people. The roles remain separate.
narrationText.D16-intro: Produce your working agreement and decision brief. Prepare a developmental working agreement and priority decision brief using fictional or sanitised information. Use the support brief, agreement, decision brief, handover record and partnership review. Identify each outstanding owner and dependency rather than invent a signature. A draft marked prepared is not submitted, assessed or proof of competence. Authenticated submission and assessor feedback remain outside this test player.. Complete T1.2 and T1.3; add the T1.1 support brief and relevant T1.4 cover record, with a short T1.5 review note. Explain dependencies rather than invent signatures.
narrationText.D16-takeaway: Key takeaway. A prepared draft is not a submission, an assessor decision or competence. Use fictional information, address all agreement areas and keep missing approvals visibly unconfirmed.

narrationText.D18-intro: Review the partnership and take it forward. Take the partnership forward. Ask whether the result is clear, whether you have authority and information, whether competing demands are resolved, and whether the work can be completed or properly handed over. Agree, work, review and revise the arrangement. Choose one improvement to your draft. Teaching progress, knowledge results and practical assessment are separate; none grants workplace authority.. Identify one improvement to your draft, review the glossary and locate the source book and reusable tools.
narrationText.D18-takeaway: Key takeaway. Keep purpose, authority, information, feasible priorities and accepted handover connected. Review the partnership when the work changes, and make one useful improvement to your draft.
narrationText.D18-p1: Purpose. Ask whether the required result is clear. Translate purpose into a defined deliverable, an owner and useful readiness evidence.
narrationText.D18-p2: Agree. Check authority, necessary information and capacity. Make personal-task limits, concern routes and other owners’ dependencies explicit.
narrationText.D18-p3: Work. Resolve competing demands through authorised choices. Distinguish request, decision, action and closure; record what remains unconfirmed.
narrationText.D18-p4: Review. Can the work be completed or properly handed over? Review one useful example and one source of friction, rather than counting how often the assistant says yes.
narrationText.D18-p5: Revise. Version agreed changes, obtain the right confirmations and communicate the current arrangement. Identify one improvement to your draft. LU2 develops authority boundaries further; this unit does not grant workplace permission.
narrationText.Q01-stem: Daniel sends invitations for a service-investment decision. Which statement best distinguishes his administrative output from the business outcome?
narrationText.Q01-a: A controlled pack with approved papers supports Lindiwe’s decision; sending invitations alone does not prove readiness.
narrationText.Q01-b: Sending the invitations proves that the investment decision has been made.
narrationText.Q01-c: Daniel must approve the investment himself to complete the administrative task.
narrationText.Q01-explanation: The EA may own the ready administrative output while the appointed executive owns the substantive decision. Activity, output and outcome are different. Source: 1.1.2 and 1.3.
narrationText.Q02-stem: A required financial appendix is still an unapproved draft before preparation. Select all appropriate actions.
narrationText.Q02-a: Identify the finance input owner and the readiness deadline.
narrationText.Q02-b: Show the missing approval and its effect on preparation to the appropriate owner and executive.
narrationText.Q02-c: Label the draft approved because its file has arrived.
narrationText.Q02-d: Seek the required decision on the gap rather than claim the pack is ready.
narrationText.Q02-explanation: Readiness needs the correct approved inputs, owners and a review point. An arrival or finished cover sheet cannot substitute for approval. Source: 1.3 and T1.1.
narrationText.Q03-stem: Match each responsibility to the role described in this fictional support arrangement. Titles can overlap in real workplaces; this is not a universal hierarchy.
narrationText.Q03-office: Own the workplace office-service arrangements where not combined.
narrationText.Q03-specialist: Make the appointed specialist decision within its professional mandate.
narrationText.Q03-explanation: The role agreement defines the work. Proximity to the executive does not transfer another role’s mandate. Source: 1.2.
narrationText.Q04-stem: Daniel can edit supplier details in the system. A supplier asks him to approve new bank details. What follows?
narrationText.Q04-b: He should route the change to the appointed finance owner and approved independent verification process.
narrationText.Q04-c: A familiar supplier needs no verification.
narrationText.Q04-explanation: Competence and access are separate from authority. The finance owner retains the approval and verification route. Source: 1.5.2 and 1.7.3 clause 5.
narrationText.Q05-stem: In the fictional Meridian agreement, which conditions support independent routine action? Select all that apply.
narrationText.Q05-a: A routine internal change is within the delegation and affects no protected commitment, external undertaking, cost or specialist dependency.
narrationText.Q05-b: Meeting consumables are pre-approved, within the approved budget and supplier process, and within the fictional R2,000 per-event limit.
narrationText.Q05-c: Two smaller purchases can be used to avoid the spending limit.
narrationText.Q05-d: Permission to place the order automatically includes payment release.
narrationText.Q05-explanation: Routine discretion is conditional. Splitting purchases is prohibited, and ordering is not payment authority. The limit is a case fact, not a workplace standard. Source: 1.5.3 and 1.7.3 clauses 4–5.
narrationText.Q06-stem: Preparation runs 09:30–10:00 and the decision meeting 10:00–10:45. How does the unaccepted supplier request for 09:45–10:15 overlap them?
narrationText.Q06-a: 15 minutes of preparation and 15 minutes of the decision meeting.
narrationText.Q06-b: 30 minutes of preparation and none of the meeting.
narrationText.Q06-c: No overlap, because a request can be added without displacing work.
narrationText.Q06-explanation: 09:45–10:00 is 15 minutes of preparation; 10:00–10:15 is 15 minutes of the decision meeting. The request is not an accepted booking. Source: 1.6.2.
narrationText.Q07-stem: A new fictional message says: “I prefer lunch at the client’s venue; Thandi has seen the request.” What can Daniel safely record?
narrationText.Q07-a: All transport and monitoring changes are confirmed.
narrationText.Q07-b: The business preference is expressed, but the required protective input, logistics and service acceptance remain to be established.
narrationText.Q07-c: The existing afternoon-visit monitoring automatically covers lunch.
narrationText.Q07-explanation: A business preference and awareness of a request do not supply separate specialist decisions or service acceptance. Source: 1.6.3. This question is not the completed later case record.
narrationText.Q08-stem: Place these states in the teaching model’s order. Use the numbered selections; each state must be used once.
narrationText.Q08-request: Define the requested result and expose constraints.
narrationText.Q08-decision: Obtain the appropriate decision and its conditions.
narrationText.Q08-action: Implement the decision and obtain required acknowledgements.
narrationText.Q08-closure: Confirm completion or an accepted transfer.
narrationText.Q08-explanation: Request, decision, action and closure need different evidence. A recommendation is not a decision and a decision is not finished implementation. Source: 1.6.4 and Figure 1.3.
narrationText.Q09-stem: Lindiwe and Daniel write “continuous monitoring” into their working agreement. What is still required?
narrationText.Q09-a: Nothing: their agreement creates the provider’s service obligation.
narrationText.Q09-b: The actual service owner must confirm the applicable mandate, coverage and assignment acceptance.
narrationText.Q09-c: Daniel should sign for the provider to complete the form.
narrationText.Q09-explanation: A working agreement operates within actual policy, authority and service contracts. Two parties cannot create another owner’s obligations. Source: 1.7.
narrationText.Q10-stem: Aisha is named as deputy, but acceptance of tonight’s assignment is missing. Which response is sound?
narrationText.Q10-a: Close the handover because a deputy exists.
narrationText.Q10-b: Assume Daniel remains personally available without limit.
narrationText.Q10-c: Record the unaccepted gap, seek the designated owner’s resolution and retain a concern route that is not solely the executive when the concern involves her.
narrationText.Q10-explanation: A transfer needs defined scope, period, access and explicit acceptance. Separate monitoring duties remain with their accepted owner. An alternative concern route is needed where the executive is involved. Source: 1.8 and T1.4.
narrationText.glossary-0: Authority. Permission to make a specified decision or perform an action within defined conditions.
narrationText.glossary-1: Commitment. Work or an arrangement that has been accepted by the appropriate party, not merely requested.
narrationText.glossary-2: Controlled record. The identified current record maintained through an agreed process, with material changes traceable.
narrationText.glossary-3: Delegation. Assignment of defined work or decision rights with scope, limits and a completion expectation.
narrationText.glossary-4: Dependency. An input, decision, resource or action on which another task depends.
narrationText.glossary-5: Executive Protection Officer (EPO). The appointed protection professional whose decisions and activities remain within the actual mandate.
narrationText.glossary-6: Handover. An explicit transfer of defined continuing work to an incoming owner who accepts it.
narrationText.glossary-7: Independent remote control room. The monitoring and coordination facility described in the programme; its powers and coverage depend on its real service mandate.
narrationText.glossary-8: Mandate. The agreed scope and authority of a role, read with the applicable organisational requirements.
narrationText.glossary-9: Priority. Work whose relative importance and timing have been considered against the agreed objectives and constraints.
narrationText.glossary-10: Protective coordination. The EA's authorised organisation of information, decisions and interfaces that support the protective arrangement.
narrationText.glossary-11: Working agreement. A practical record of how the executive-support partnership operates within existing authority and policy.

narrationText.welcome: A professional executive partnership makes work clear and commitments reliable. In this unit you will translate priorities into support deliverables, prepare a usable working agreement, distinguish role boundaries, present options when demands conflict, and arrange a concern route and sustainable cover. Your two main work products are a working agreement and a priority decision brief. The Meridian people and arrangements are fictional. Numerical examples are case facts, not operating standards. The course does not grant workplace authority. You will follow Daniel as he supports Lindiwe at Meridian. Start with the facts available at 07:40, make your own first brief, and only then compare the later confirmed record. Use the glossary for unfamiliar words and the source reading for detail. Practice activities help you learn without adding to your formal mark. The separate formative test lets you try the agreed question and quiz retry rules. Keep your practical portfolio as a draft for later feedback. You can pause or replay narration and read the same material as text. Use only fictional or sanitised information in your responses.
